{{Short description|Filmography of American filmmaker}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=April 2025}}
[[File:Paul Thomas Anderson 2007 crop.jpg|thumb|Anderson in 2007]]

[[Paul Thomas Anderson]] is an American filmmaker. He has directed ten feature-length films, five short films, twenty three music videos, two documentaries, one television episode as a guest segment director, and one theatrical play. He made his directorial debut with the [[mockumentary]] short film ''[[The Dirk Diggler Story]]'' (1988), at the age of 18, about a fictional well-endowed [[pornographic actor]] in the 1970s.<ref name="NYTimes">{{cite web|last1=Hirschberg|first1=Lynn|title=His Way|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/12/19/magazine/his-way.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm|website=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=December 19, 1999}}</ref> Anderson followed it five years later with another short film, ''[[Cigarettes & Coffee]]'' (1993). Anderson wrote and directed the crime film ''[[Hard Eight (film)|Hard Eight]]'' (1996), starring [[Philip Baker Hall]], [[John C. Reilly]], [[Gwyneth Paltrow]] and [[Samuel L. Jackson]]. The film was well received.<ref name="RottenTomatoes">{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/celebrity/paul_thomas_anderson |title=Paul Thomas Anderson |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=([[NBCUniversal]] & [[Warner Bros.]]) |access-date=June 21, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author1=Roger Ebert|author-link=Roger Ebert|title=Hard Eight Movie Review & Film Summary|url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/hard-eight-1997|website=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|publisher=([[Sun-Times Media Group]])|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=February 27, 1997}}</ref> Using the basis of ''The Dirk Diggler Story'', Anderson wrote and directed an expansion of the film, ''[[Boogie Nights]]'' (1997).<ref>{{cite web|last1=McKenna|first1=Kristine|title=Knows It When He Sees It|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-oct-12-ca-41788-story.html|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=October 12, 1997}}</ref> It stars [[Mark Wahlberg]] as an actor in the [[Golden Age of Porn]] from the 1970s to the 1980s. The film received acclaim from critics and was a commercial success;<ref name=NYTimes/> at the [[70th Academy Awards]] ceremony, the film was nominated for three [[Academy Awards]], including for [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor|Best Supporting Actor]] ([[Burt Reynolds]]), [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress|Best Supporting Actress]] ([[Julianne Moore]]) and [[Academy Award for Writing Original Screenplay|Best Original Screenplay]].<ref name=nom70aa>{{cite web|url=http://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/1998 |title=Oscars Ceremonies 1998 |access-date=June 21, 2016 |work=[[Academy Award|Oscars.org]]|date=October 5, 2014 |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]}}</ref>

His 1999 ensemble film ''[[Magnolia (film)|Magnolia]]'' followed four intertwined and peculiar stories in the [[San Fernando Valley]].<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Schickel|first1=Richard|title=Cinema: Magnolia|url=http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,992979,00.html|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|publisher=([[Time Inc.]])|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=December 27, 1999}}</ref> The film was another critical success for Anderson and at the [[72nd Academy Awards]], it was nominated for three Academy Awards, including for Best Actor in a Supporting Role ([[Tom Cruise]]), [[Academy Award for Best Original Song|Best Original Song]] for "Save Me" by Aimee Mann and Best Original Screenplay.<ref name=nom72aa>{{cite web|url=http://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2000 |title=Oscars Ceremonies 2000 |access-date=June 21, 2016 |work=[[Academy Award|Oscars.org]]|date=April 22, 2015 |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]}}</ref> Anderson directed the romantic comedy-drama ''[[Punch-Drunk Love]]'' (2002), starring [[Adam Sandler]] as a lonely man with anger issues.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Bradshaw|first1=Peter|title=Punch-Drunk Love|url=https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2003/feb/07/artsfeatures1|website=[[The Guardian]]|publisher=([[Guardian Media Group]])|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=February 7, 2003}}</ref> He went on to write and direct ''[[There Will Be Blood]]'' (2007), based loosely on [[Upton Sinclair]]'s novel ''[[Oil!]]'' The film was critically acclaimed, winning numerous awards. It was nominated for seven [[80th Academy Awards|Academy Awards]], including Best Director and Best Picture, with [[Daniel Day-Lewis]] winning Best Actor.<ref name=nom80aa>{{cite web|url=http://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2008 |title=Oscars Ceremonies 2008 |access-date=June 21, 2016 |work=[[Academy Award|Oscars.org]]|date=October 7, 2014 |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]}}</ref> After a five-year hiatus, he directed the 2012 film ''[[The Master (2012 film)|The Master]]'' starring [[Joaquin Phoenix]] and [[Philip Seymour Hoffman]]. The film's fictional movement "The Cause" was widely compared to the real-life religion of [[Scientology]] in the media, despite not directly referencing it.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pilkington|first1=Ed|title=Church of Scientology snaps up Hollywood film studio|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2011/apr/26/scientology-hollywood-film-studio|website=[[The Guardian]]|publisher=([[Guardian Media Group]])|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=April 26, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Brown|first1=Lane|title=So This New Paul Thomas Anderson Movie Is Definitely About Scientology, Right?|url=https://www.vulture.com/2009/12/so_this_new_paul_thomas_anders.html|website=Vulture|publisher=([[New York (magazine)|New York Magazine]])|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=December 3, 2009}}</ref>

Anderson adapted [[Thomas Pynchon]]'s 2009 novel ''[[Inherent Vice]]'' into a film of the [[Inherent Vice (film)|same name]] in 2014. Joaquin Phoenix played a [[Drug culture|stoner]] [[hippie]] and [[private investigator]] investigating a case involving the disappearance of his ex-girlfriend and her wealthy boyfriend.<ref>{{cite web|author1=NPR Stff|title=Adapting 'Inherent Vice' Made Director Feel Like A Student Again|url=https://www.npr.org/2014/12/13/369599571/adapting-inherent-vice-made-director-felt-like-a-student-again|website=[[NPR]]|publisher=(National Public Radio, Inc.)|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=December 13, 2014}}</ref> In 2015, he directed the documentary ''[[Junun (film)|Junun]]'' about the making of [[Junun (album)|album of the same name]] in [[Mehrangarh Fort]], [[Rajasthan]], India by the Israeli composer [[Shye Ben Tzur]], English composer and [[Radiohead]] guitarist [[Jonny Greenwood]], Indian ensemble the Rajasthan Express, and Radiohead producer [[Nigel Godrich]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Rooney|first1=David|title='Junun': NYFF Review|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/review/paul-thomas-andersons-junun-nyff-830826|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|publisher=([[Prometheus Global Media]])|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=October 8, 2015}}</ref> ''[[Phantom Thread]]'' (2017) starred Day-Lewis as a renowned dressmaker in the 1950s. The film was nominated for six Academy Awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] and [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]] for Anderson. Anderson's ninth film, ''[[Licorice Pizza]]'' (2021), was released to great acclaim, earning him the [[BAFTA Award for Best Original Screenplay]], in addition to nominations for three Academy Awards and two Golden Globes. His tenth film, ''[[One Battle After Another]]'', was released in September 2025.

He has directed music videos for such artists as [[Fiona Apple]], [[Haim (band)|Haim]], [[Aimee Mann]], [[Joanna Newsom]] and Radiohead.<ref name="Music-Videos">{{cite magazine|last1=Kaufman|first1=Gil|title=Paul Thomas Anderson's Music Videos: 11 Clips From Radiohead, Fiona Apple, Joanna Newsom & More|url=https://www.billboard.com/articles/news/7358055/radiohead-daydreaming-director-paul-thomas-anderson-other-music-videos|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|publisher=([[Prometheus Global Media]])|access-date=June 21, 2016|date=May 9, 2012}}</ref>
